after your last trial, and the notebook teaches you to report that result plainly,
including when nothing beats the base rate.
By the end you will be able to:
explain the steps of a supervised analysis (framing → data → split → train → validate → refine → test → justify) and name the failure each step guards against;
build and validate a classification model on a climate-model ensemble, reporting precision, recall and a confusion matrix;
compare refinement trials as a paired test across runs, so a gap inside the run-to-run spread is not read as a difference;
justify the chosen model honestly on measured performance and cost, including when nothing beats the base rate.

A supervised classifier on CESM2 LENS

. Part 1 frames the question as a
decision. Part 2 locates the data through the

catalogue and fills a Metadata Document, explores the target and the
input, and splits by ensemble member. Part 3 climbs a three-rung ladder (logistic regression → decision tree → gradient boosting)
against the base rate and a one-rule classifier; validates with a confusion matrix, precision and recall; runs refinement trials
as a paired test; tests once; and ends with a written justification.

The signal is weak, and it is not the one the physical prior predicts: in the committed table, El Niño
autumns are followed by slightly fewer wet winters than the base rate, moderate La Niña autumns by more, and the strongest La Niña
by fewer. The Niño-sign rule therefore sits below the base rate, a linear model can only learn a sign (the logistic rung at the
base-rate threshold is close to the sign rule reversed), and a boosting model, which can bend with the relation, scores above the
base rate on validation folds at the base-rate decision threshold (at the default 0.5 it calls almost nothing wet). Registering it as a trial and running the held-out test are the learner’s to do. The limits are stated up front: a
model-world study (CESM2 winters scored against CESM2 winters, never against observations, with CESM2’s own ENSO and
teleconnection), on a ~1° grid that smooths the Front Range’s orography, in a default season (DJF) that NWS Boulder does not name
as El Niño’s wet season east of the Divide. A result here is not a result for the real Front Range; the Summary names the change
that would test that.

Funding: self-funded. This cookbook has not been reviewed or sponsored by NSF NCAR or NSF Unidata; it is offered to the
Project Pythia community for its own review.

Drafting: Drafted with AI assistance (Anthropic’s Claude) from cited sources, under the author’s direction, and reviewed by the author in several full read-throughs. Text and code were checked against those sources and the notebooks’ own outputs by automated tests and independent AI reviewers; no human subject-matter expert has reviewed it yet.

How it was checked (as of 2026-10-29): the notebook and handbook rest on 18 source records in the author’s research
library, each with its licence and retrieval date, 15 with the exact passages quoted; every prose paragraph of 40 words or
more must cite one. Automated checks, each tested by planting an error it must catch, gate template conformance, sources,
links, licences, accessibility and a full strict build. Independent AI reviewers read it as a Project Pythia advocate and as
a skeptical Earth system scientist over five rounds; a finding was acted on only after it was reproduced, by re-running the
code or fetching the source. They caught real errors, among them an overstated result that is now corrected. A human
subject-matter review has not happened yet and is welcome.
